    columns={"num_epochs": "configured_max_epochs"}
)

finetuning_runtime_display["actual_epochs_run"] = (
    finetuning_runtime_display["scenario"].map(
        {
            scenario: len(result["history"]["train_loss"])
            for scenario, result in finetuned_results.items()
        }
    )
)

This section summarises the computational cost of fully retraining a new model from each retain set. These runtimes provide the reference against which retain-set fine-tuning is compared.

8.3 Runtime Comparison¶

The runtime comparison table reports the time taken by fine-tuning and full retraining for each deletion scenario. This supports later discussion of computational trade-offs.

In [82]:

)

Retain-set fine-tuning was slower than full retraining in four of the five scenarios. Runtime was approximately equal in S2, with a ratio of 0.99. Across all scenarios, runtime ratios ranged from 0.99 to 2.21, with a median of 1.32. Retain-set fine-tuning therefore did not provide a consistent computational advantage under the configurations used. These results represent the observed cost of each method rather than a strictly controlled benchmark because the methods used different batch sizes and training settings.

8.4 Epoch Selection Analysis¶

This section compares the checkpoint selected using validation loss with the checkpoints that most closely match the fully retrained model according to probability, loss and entropy. Epoch 0 is excluded from checkpoint selection because it represents the unchanged baseline model and has not performed unlearning.

The runtime reported for the validation-selected model is the total time required to complete training and early stopping. It is not the runtime at the selected checkpoint itself.

In [83]:
# 8.4 Checkpoint-selection analysis

selection_rows = []

for scenario in scenario_names:
    scenario_results = (
        retain_epoch_sweep_results[
            retain_epoch_sweep_results["scenario"] == scenario
        ]
        .set_index("epoch")
        .sort_index()
    )

    # Epoch 0 is the unchanged baseline, not an unlearning checkpoint.
    candidate_results = scenario_results.loc[
        scenario_results.index >= 1
    ]

    best_probability_epoch = int(
        candidate_results[
            "forget_probability_mae_to_retraining"
        ].idxmin()
    )
    best_loss_epoch = int(
        candidate_results[
            "forget_loss_mae_to_retraining"
        ].idxmin()
    )
    best_entropy_epoch = int(
        candidate_results[
            "forget_entropy_mae_to_retraining"
        ].idxmin()
    )

    validation_selected_epoch = int(
        finetuned_results[scenario]["best_epoch"]
    )
    actual_epochs_run = len(
        finetuned_results[scenario]["history"]["train_loss"]
    )
    finetuning_runtime = float(
        finetuned_results[scenario]["runtime_seconds"]
    )

    full_runtime_row = runtime_comparison.loc[
        runtime_comparison["scenario"] == scenario,
        "runtime_seconds_retrained",
    ]
    full_retraining_runtime = float(full_runtime_row.iloc[0])

    sweep_epochs = {
        best_probability_epoch,
        best_loss_epoch,
        best_entropy_epoch,
    }

    selection_rows.append(
        {
            "scenario": scenario,
            "display_name": scenario_display_names.get(
                scenario,
                scenario,
            ),
            "validation_selected_epoch": validation_selected_epoch,
            "best_probability_epoch": best_probability_epoch,
            "best_loss_epoch": best_loss_epoch,
            "best_entropy_epoch": best_entropy_epoch,
            "sweep_criteria_select_same_epoch": len(sweep_epochs) == 1,
            "actual_finetuning_epochs_run": actual_epochs_run,
            "finetuning_runtime_seconds": finetuning_runtime,
            "full_retraining_runtime_seconds": full_retraining_runtime,
            "runtime_ratio_finetuned_to_retrained": (
                finetuning_runtime / full_retraining_runtime
            ),
        }
    )

Probability, loss and entropy selected the same positive fine-tuning checkpoint in all five scenarios: epoch 2 for S1–S4 and epoch 5 for S5. The validation-loss selection matched this checkpoint only for S1. This difference is expected because validation loss selects the checkpoint that best preserves general predictive performance, whereas the epoch-sweep criteria select the checkpoint most similar to full retraining on the forget set. The epoch numbers are compared descriptively because the validation experiment and epoch sweep use separate training trajectories.

8.5 Computational Evaluation Summary¶

This section summarises the observed runtime of retain-set fine-tuning and full retraining. It includes the actual number of epochs completed so that runtime differences can be interpreted alongside the amount of training performed.

The comparison represents the runtime of each method under its selected configuration. It is not a strictly controlled benchmark because fine-tuning and full retraining use different batch sizes, learning rates and early-stopping settings.

9. Save Evaluation Outputs¶

This section saves the models, metrics, predictions, comparison tables and figures produced by the notebook. Saving these outputs does not form part of the computational evaluation; it preserves the results for later analysis and reporting.

Save fine-tuned models

Each selected fine-tuned model checkpoint is saved with its scenario metadata. These checkpoints are the model artefacts produced by the retain-set fine-tuning method.

            "num_epochs": result["num_epochs"],

            "early_stopping_triggered": result["early_stopping_triggered"],
            "runtime_seconds": result["runtime_seconds"],
            "source_checkpoint": str(baseline_paths["baseline_model"]),
        },
        model_path,
    )

10. Discussion¶

The discussion section interprets the results produced above. It follows the dissertation narrative from behavioural evidence, to utility preservation, to forgetfulness diagnostics and computational cost.

10.1 Overall Comparison¶

The following cells prepare visual summaries and scenario-level tables for the discussion. These outputs support the written interpretation that follows.

In [95]:

Behavioural findings

Retain-set fine-tuning produced models that remained generally close to the corresponding fully retrained models. Across the complete test set, prediction agreement ranged from approximately 98.35% to 98.99%, while the mean absolute probability difference remained below 0.016 in every scenario. These values show that the models behaved similarly overall, although high agreement alone does not demonstrate forgetting because the original baseline model was also close to full retraining in several scenarios.

The forget-set comparison provides a more detailed picture. In S1, prediction agreement with full retraining remained unchanged at 98.83%, while probability distance increased slightly from 0.0109 to 0.0110. Fine-tuning therefore provided no meaningful behavioural improvement in this scenario. S2 showed a small improvement: agreement increased from 98.42% to 98.65%, and probability distance decreased from 0.0134 to 0.0117.

The result for S3 was mixed. Prediction agreement improved from 98.53% to 98.70%, but probability distance increased from 0.0131 to 0.0141. This means that more class labels matched full retraining, but the underlying predicted probabilities did not become closer. S4 showed a small deterioration on both measures, with agreement decreasing from 98.51% to 98.36% and probability distance increasing from 0.0146 to 0.0151.

S5 provided the clearest behavioural improvement. Agreement with full retraining increased from 94.57% for the baseline model to 96.04% after fine-tuning, while probability distance decreased from 0.0361 to 0.0278. S5 created a larger initial difference between the baseline and fully retrained models because its forget set represented a structured and distributionally distinct group. Fine-tuning therefore had a clearer change to reproduce than in the random-deletion scenarios.

The epoch sweep also showed that checkpoint selection affects the result. Probability, loss and entropy selected epoch 2 as the best positive fine-tuning checkpoint for S1–S4 and epoch 5 for S5. However, the validation-selected checkpoint matched this choice only in S1. Validation loss selects the model with the best general predictive performance, whereas the other criteria select the model most similar to full retraining on the forget set. Utility-based early stopping may therefore preserve performance without selecting the checkpoint that provides the strongest unlearning evidence.

The different behavioural measures did not always agree. Distribution-level Wasserstein distance moved closer to full retraining in four scenarios, whereas record-level probability and prediction-agreement measures produced more mixed results. This is not necessarily contradictory: two models can have similar overall output distributions while assigning different probabilities to individual records. Behavioural evidence should therefore be considered across multiple measurements.

Utility findings

Retain-set fine-tuning preserved predictive utility in all five scenarios. Test accuracy remained between 85.60% and 85.83%, F1 score remained between 0.6731 and 0.6782, and AUROC remained close to 0.910.

Compared with the original baseline, changes in accuracy, F1 score and AUROC were small. The largest reduction in F1 score was approximately 0.20 percentage points in S2, while the largest improvement was approximately 0.31 percentage points in S4. AUROC was effectively unchanged across all scenarios.

The fine-tuned models also remained close to their fully retrained references. F1 differences did not exceed approximately 1.01 percentage points, and AUROC differences did not exceed approximately 0.12 percentage points. These results show that retain-set fine-tuning did not meaningfully damage the model’s ability to predict income on unseen test records.

Utility preservation must nevertheless be separated from evidence of forgetting. A model can retain high accuracy while continuing to behave like the original baseline on the forget records. The utility results demonstrate that fine-tuning is safe in terms of predictive performance, but they do not establish that unlearning was successful.

Forgetfulness findings

Entropy provided scenario-dependent evidence. For the validation-selected checkpoints, relative entropy improvement was negative for S1, S2, S3 and S4. This means that the entropy values moved further from those of full retraining rather than closer. The random scenarios therefore did not provide entropy-based evidence of forgetting at their selected checkpoints.

S3 showed some potential during the epoch sweep. Epoch 2 improved entropy distance by approximately 12.53%, but the validation-selected checkpoint was epoch 4, where the relative improvement was negative. This reinforces the finding that validation loss does not necessarily select the checkpoint with the strongest forget-set similarity.

S5 produced the strongest entropy evidence. Its validation-selected checkpoint improved entropy distance to full retraining by approximately 23.95%, while epoch 5 produced an improvement of approximately 39.45%. A majority of S5 forget records also moved closer to the fully retrained entropy values. Together with the behavioural results, this provides evidence that fine-tuning reduced the difference between the baseline and retrained models for S5.

The membership-inference results cannot be used as evidence of successful forgetting. Loss-based attack AUROC was close to chance for S1–S4, while S5 produced an elevated value of approximately 0.596. However, the fully retrained S5 model produced a similarly elevated result of approximately 0.593. This suggests that the attack was detecting the unusual distribution of the S5 cohort rather than whether those records were used during training.

More importantly, the deliberately overfitted positive-control model produced an AUROC of only 0.4899. The attack therefore failed to detect membership even when a stronger membership signal was expected. As a result, all membership-inference findings must be treated as inconclusive. Near-chance MIA performance cannot demonstrate forgetting when the attack itself has not been shown to work reliably in this experimental setting.

Overall, the forgetfulness evidence is strongest for S5, limited for S3 and weak or absent for the random scenarios. Even for S5, the results provide empirical evidence consistent with approximate unlearning rather than proof that the influence of every forget record has been removed.

Scenario Overall interpretation
S1 – Random 1% Utility was preserved, but behavioural and entropy results provided no meaningful evidence of forgetting.
S2 – Random 5% Utility was preserved and behaviour improved slightly, but entropy did not move closer to full retraining.
S3 – Provider withdrawal Behavioural results were mixed. Entropy improved at epoch 2, but not at the validation-selected checkpoint.
S4 – Random 10% Utility was preserved, but forget-set behaviour and entropy were slightly worse than the baseline reference.
S5 – Retention expiry Strongest evidence: behaviour and entropy both moved towards full retraining, although MIA remained inconclusive.

Computational findings

Retain-set fine-tuning did not provide a consistent computational advantage. It was slower than full retraining in four of the five scenarios, while runtime was approximately equal in S2. Runtime ratios ranged from 0.99 to 2.21, with a median of 1.32.

These results should not be interpreted as showing that fine-tuning is inherently slower than full retraining. Fine-tuning used a batch size of 64, while full retraining used a batch size of 256. The methods also used different learning rates and early-stopping settings. The results therefore represent the observed cost of each configured method rather than a strictly controlled runtime benchmark.

10.2 Limitations¶

The evaluation uses full retraining as an empirical reference, but similarity to full retraining is not a formal guarantee that all influence of the forget records has been removed. Entropy, probability distance, loss distance and prediction agreement are all derived from model outputs and should not be treated as independent proof of deletion.

The random forget sets also created a difficult evaluation setting. Randomly removing 1%, 5% or 10% of the training data produced fully retrained models that were already very similar to the original baseline. Consequently, there was little measurable difference for fine-tuning to reproduce. A lack of improvement in these scenarios does not necessarily mean that fine-tuning performed no update, but it does mean that the selected measurements cannot provide strong evidence of forgetting.

The S5 scenario produced clearer changes because its forget set was distributionally different from the retain set. This made behavioural and entropy differences easier to observe, but it also confounded membership inference because an attack could distinguish the cohort distribution rather than training membership.

The MIA positive control failed, so the membership-inference results cannot support conclusions about whether membership information was removed. Runtime measurements were also based on different method-specific configurations and individual experimental runs, limiting the strength of the computational comparison.

Finally, the results apply to one dataset, model architecture and unlearning method. Further experiments using repeated training seeds, additional datasets and alternative unlearning methods would be required to determine whether the findings generalise.

10.3 Answer to the Research Question¶

Retain-set fine-tuning preserved predictive utility across all five deletion scenarios, but the evidence of approximate unlearning was mixed and depended strongly on the forget-set design.

The random-deletion scenarios produced little separation between the baseline and fully retrained models, making successful forgetting difficult to demonstrate. S3 showed limited evidence at an alternative checkpoint, while S5 produced the clearest movement towards full retraining across both behavioural and entropy measurements. Membership inference did not provide reliable evidence because its positive control failed.

Retain-set fine-tuning can therefore be described as a utility-preserving approximate unlearning baseline that provides scenario-dependent evidence of forgetting. It should not be presented as a method that consistently reproduces full retraining or guarantees complete deletion.

10.4 Conclusion¶

Retain-set fine-tuning maintained model performance but did not consistently reproduce the behaviour of full retraining. Evidence was weakest for the random deletion scenarios, where the baseline and fully retrained models were already highly similar, and strongest for the structured retention-expiry scenario.

The experiment also demonstrates why unlearning should not be evaluated using a single measurement. Utility remained stable even when behavioural and entropy evidence was weak, while MIA was inconclusive because the positive control failed. The most defensible conclusion is that retain-set fine-tuning provides partial and scenario-dependent evidence of approximate unlearning, with S5 showing the clearest result.

These findings do not establish formal deletion, privacy guarantees or GDPR compliance. They provide an empirical assessment of whether the fine-tuned model behaves more like a model retrained without the forget records.
